newsitem.title: NORWAY: Norway fin min says opposition would lift spending.
newsitem.headline: Norway fin min says opposition would lift spending.

text.p: Finance Minister Jens Stoltenberg, in an interview published on Thursday, accused the opposition of wanting to ruin the Norwegian economy by proposing to increase spending.
Stoltenberg told financial daily Dagens Naeringsliv that the financial markets had reason to fear a government coalition made up of the three centrist parties in parliament.
The ruling Labour Party minority government has lost ground in recent opinion polls. Norway holds parliamentary elections on September 15.

"The centrist parties would ruin the Norwegian economy," Stoltenberg said. "They want to increase spending practically everywhere. If the economic proposals of the centrist parties were to be carried out we would be facing an interest rate hike."

The newspaper said the centrist parties -- the Christian People's Party, the Centre Party and liberal Venstre -- wanted to increase net spending by between six and nine billion crowns a year compared to the 1997 government budget.
Kjell Magne Bondevik, prime minister candidate for the Christian People's Party, said concern in the market about a possible centrist government was based on a misunderstanding.
"There has hardly been a more responsible opposition party than the Christian People's Party," he told Dagens Naeringsliv.
Bondevik said a centrist government would be able to maintain a reasonable balance between spending and income.
The crown has weakened considerably recently.
Market players attribute the fall to higher-than-expected inflation figures for May, weaker oil prices and growing concern over the outcome of the election, based on recent opinion polls.

The centrist parties want to join forces in a new minority government should they mobilise enough votes at the polls to beat the Labour Party, which hovered around 30 percent in voter support in surveys published this week.
In the 1993 parliamentary election, Labour received 36.9 percent of the votes.
